name: Phase Two: Choose the Pilot
title: Phase Two: Choose the Pilot
answer: Phase Two of a school AI rollout means choosing a first pilot that begins with a clearly defined problem rather than a product, and keeping that pilot low in risk and high in visibility. It matters because starting from a product usually produces a solution looking for a problem, while a safe early success builds the habits and trust needed for harder work later.

sections.body: This phase asks a district to name the problem first, such as teachers spending too long on parent messages, ninth graders failing algebra at an alarming rate, or too much cafeteria food being thrown away. With the problem clear, the district can seek tools that address it and set aside those that do not. Beginning with a product tends to end with a solution searching for a problem. The pilot itself should be low in risk and high in visibility so that early wins are seen and shared. Drafting tools for teachers, translation for routine family messages, and practice tools with teacher oversight are offered as good first choices.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, the pilot is chosen by matching a tool to the named problem and to the level of risk the school can absorb. Drafting tools for teachers, translation for routine family messages, and practice tools with teacher oversight are the suggested starting points. Tools that flag students, score work for grades, or collect sensitive data are held back until a few simpler pilots have been run well. The text does not give separate grade band guidance beyond the examples it uses, such as ninth graders failing algebra. Success with a small, safe pilot is what builds the habits and trust a harder one will need.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea through the practice of piloting rather than presenting a study of it. Its one cited support is that researchers have proposed frameworks for judging educational AI on responsibility as well as performance, including accuracy, fairness, transparency, and data protection (Lin et al., 2026). The text adds that a district does not need a formal framework to ask the basic questions, and it points to Figure 4.4 for the evidence and privacy criteria a vendor should be able to answer in writing. No further study, figure, or finding is given for the pilot choice itself.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits set out in the text are about risk and timing. Tools that flag students, score work for grades, or collect sensitive data should wait until the district has run a few simpler pilots well. Vendors should be judged on evidence and privacy rather than on the demo, and the criteria in Figure 4.4 are things a vendor should be able to answer in writing. The decisions about which problem to name, which tool to try, and when a harder pilot is warranted stay with the district and its people. Nothing here is legal advice, and the text describes practice rather than rules.
